passages.title: The unlettered Prophet as Allah's favour
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat open Sūrat al-Jumuʿah by setting one small, unlettered community against the backdrop of the entire universe. Ayah 1 has everything in the heavens and the earth glorifying Allah; ayat 2–3 then narrow to a single point in history — a Messenger raised among a people who could not read — and ayah 4 names the whole thing for what it is: *faḍl Allāh*, Allah's grace, bestowed on whom He wills. The thread holding the passage together is that the coming of Muhammad ﷺ is an act of the King, the Holy, the Almighty, the All-Wise.

**A note on where we are.** Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Hurayrah narrated that Allah's Messenger ﷺ used to recite Sūrat al-Jumuʿah and Sūrat al-Munāfiqūn during the Friday Prayer — Muslim collected this in his Ṣaḥīḥ. So these are ayat the Prophet ﷺ himself put in front of his community week after week.

## Ayah 1: the universe is already busy praising Him

Ibn Kathir states plainly that everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah's praises — **all types of living creatures and inanimate objects alike** — and he brings the parallel from Sūrat al-Isrāʾ: *"there is not a thing but glorifies His praise"* (17:44).

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān pushes on what that actually means. It is easy enough, he says, to take it symbolically: every single particle Allah created bears testimony in its "circumstantial language" to the wisdom and power of the Wise Creator, and that testimony is its tasbīḥ. But the fact is, he argues, that everything performs tasbīḥ **in its real sense**, in its own way — because Allah has bestowed some sort of sense and perception on every particle of this universe, even on stones and trees, according to their ability. And since the first demand upon sense and perception is that a creature recognise its Creator and Maker and glorify Him, it is not far-fetched to conceive that things really do declare Allah's purity in their own peculiar language, even though human ears might not be able to hear it. That is exactly what the Qurʾān says at the end of the same ayah: *"but you do not understand their extolling"* (17:44).

**Why "yusabbiḥu" and not "sabbaḥa".** This is a detail worth slowing down for. Sūrahs of the Qurʾān that begin with *sabbaḥa* or *yusabbiḥu* are called the **Musabbiḥāt**, and in all of them the same truth is established: everything in the heavens and the earth proclaims the purity of Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes that at the commencement of most of the Musabbiḥāt the past-tense form *sabbaḥa* is employed; only at the beginning of al-Jumuʿah and at-Taghābun is the present form *yusabbiḥu* used. The different forms, he says, carry a fresh rhetorical elegance and refinement. **The past tense connotes certitude** — which is why it is mostly used. **The present form connotes continuity** — and that is why it is employed in these two places. Choosing the continuous form here means the reader steps into an ongoing act: as you read this ayah, creation is mid-praise.

**The four names.** The ayah does not simply say "glorifies Allah" and stop; it stacks four descriptions of the One being glorified.

- **الْمَلِك**, the King — Ibn Kathir: He is the Owner and King of the heavens and the earth, who has perfect control over their affairs.
- **al-Quddūs**, the Holy — He is free of all shortcomings; His attributes are perfect.
- **al-ʿAzīz**, the Almighty, and **al-Ḥakīm**, the All-Wise — Ibn Kathir passes over these quickly here, noting that their explanation has already been discussed in many places.

Hold those last two names in mind. They return at the end of ayah 3, and there Ibn Kathir explains their force: Allah is Almighty and All-Wise **in His legislation and in the destiny He appoints**. The Sovereign who has all power is also the One whose decisions are wise — which bears directly on ayat 2–4 and where, and among whom, He chose to send His final Messenger.

## Ayat 2–3: a Messenger among the unlettered

**Who are "the unlettered"?** Ibn Kathir: the word *ummiyyīn* here refers to the Arabs, and he cites the ayah where the two groups are set side by side — *"those who were given the Scripture and those who are illiterates"* (3:20). Maʿārif ul Qurʾān explains the word itself: *ummiyyīn* is the plural of *ummiyy*, which denotes "unlettered". The Arabs were known by this title because they did not know how to read and write; very few of them had the knowledge of reading and writing.

**Why mention it at all?** Because, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān says, the Arabs are specially referred to here in order to express the great power of Allah. Look at what the ayah goes on to list as the Messenger's work — recitation, purification, teaching the Book and the Wisdom. The duties and reformative functions of a Prophet are based on knowledge and education. These are reforms **no unlettered individual could ever teach, nor is it possible for an unlettered nation to learn**. And the Messenger raised among them was himself unlettered. It was only through the Divine Supreme Power and the miracle of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that, once these reforms began, great scholars, intellectuals, men of letters, savants and sages were born among that unlettered people, and their knowledge, wisdom, sagacity and erudition came to be recognised by the entire world. The improbability is the point.

**"A Messenger from among themselves."** Ibn Kathir reads this ayah as testifying that Allah accepted the invocation of His friend Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, when he supplicated Allah to send to the people of Makkah a Messenger from among their own — one who would recite Allah's statements to them, purify them, and teach them the Book and the Ḥikmah. The wording of ayah 2 is nearly the wording of that supplication. Prophethood arriving in Makkah was a prayer being answered.

**And it arrived at the lowest point.** Ibn Kathir describes the moment: Allah sent him **when the Messengers had ceased and the way was obscure** — indeed, a time when it was most needed. He is unsparing about the state of the world then: Allah hated the people of the earth, Arabs and non-Arabs alike, except for a few of the People of the Scripture who kept to the true faith Allah sent to ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, peace be upon him. As for the Arabs specifically, in ancient times they used to adhere to the religion of Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him; they later changed it, corrupted it and contradicted it — **choosing polytheism instead of tawḥīd and doubts instead of certainty** — inventing a religion that Allah did not legislate, just as the People of the Scriptures did when they changed and corrupted their Divine Books.

Into that, Ibn Kathir says, Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ with a great divine legislation, a perfect religion suitable for all humans and jinn: in it there is guidance and explanation of all that they need in this life and the Hereafter; it draws them closer to Paradise and Allah's pleasure and takes them away from the Fire and Allah's anger; and in it is the final judgement for all types of doubts and suspicion, in all major and minor matters of the religion. In Muhammad ﷺ, he writes, Allah gathered all the good qualities of the Prophets before him and gave him what He has never given the earlier and later generations of mankind. May Allah's peace and blessings be on him until the Day of Judgement.

## The three tasks the Messenger ﷺ was sent to do

Ayah 2 lists them in order: *he recites to them His verses, purifies them, and teaches them the Book and the Wisdom.* Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes that these are two things at once — three divine blessings bestowed on mankind, and simultaneously **the basic objectives and terms of reference of the Prophet ﷺ**, for which he was sent into this world.

**1. Recitation — *yatlū ʿalayhim āyātih*.** The word *tilāwah* lexically signifies "to follow, to obey"; in the terminology of the Qurʾān it signifies the recitation or reading of the Divine Words. "His verses" here refers to the verses of the Qurʾān, and the prepositional phrase *ʿalayhim*, "to them", signifies that one of the Prophet's duties is to recite those verses **to the people**.

**2. Purification — *yuzakkīhim*.** From *tazkiyah*, "to make pure". Maʿārif ul Qurʾān explains that the word is often used exclusively for **inner** cleanliness — being free of such adulterating matter as kufr and shirk, and free of inner moral defilement — but that it is occasionally used in the general sense of both outer and inner cleanliness, and probably carries that general sense here. So the Messenger's work covers a person's body and dress as well as his faith, his actions and his moral attitude.

**3. Teaching the Book and the Wisdom — *yuʿallimuhum al-kitāba wal-ḥikmah*.** *Al-Kitāb* refers to the Holy Qurʾān. *Al-Ḥikmah* refers to all the teachings and guidance received from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, orally or practically — which is why, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes, many commentators have interpreted *ḥikmah* as the **Sunnah**, the Approved Way. Anyone who imagines the Prophet's ﷺ role stops at delivering the text is reading only one of the three verbs.

**A puzzle in the order.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān raises it: the natural order would be (1) recitation of the words, (2) teaching of the meaning, and consequently (3) making pure by inculcating righteous deeds and high morals. Yet in most places the Qurʾān changes that sequence, inserting *tazkiyah* **between** recitation and teaching. Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī explains that if the natural order had been maintained in all verses, all three elements would have combined together and become "one" — as happens in the pharmaceutical mixing of many substances, where the aggregate loses the separate identity of each element and becomes a single compound. Probably, Allah wanted the Divine blessings and the three prophetic duties to remain **separately identifiable**, and by changing the natural order in most places the Qurʾān has alluded to this.

## Ayah 3: "and others among them who have not yet joined them"

This is the ayah that pulls later readers into the passage. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān: *ākharīn* means "other people", and *lammā yalḥaqū bihim* means those who have not yet joined the unlettered people. It refers to **all those Muslims who will enter the fold of Islam until the Last Hour** — as transmitted by Ibn Zayd, Mujāhid and others. This indicates that the succeeding generations of Muslims will be appended to the earlier generations of believers, that is, the noble Companions. Rūḥ calls this **great good news for the succeeding generations of Muslims**.

**The moment it was revealed.** Abū Hurayrah said: "We were sitting with the Prophet ﷺ when Sūrat al-Jumuʿah was revealed to him." When the ayah *"and others among them who have not yet joined them"* was reached, they said, "Who are they, O Allah's Messenger?" The Prophet ﷺ did not reply until they had repeated the question three times. Salmān al-Fārisī was with them at that time — and Allah's Messenger ﷺ placed his hand on Salmān and said: *"If faith were on ath-Thurayyā (the Pleiades), even then some men — or a man — from these people would attain it."* Ibn Kathir records this from Imam Abū ʿAbdillāh al-Bukhārī, may Allah have mercy on him, and notes that Muslim, at-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʾī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Jarīr also collected it. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān records the same narration as being in Bukhārī and Muslim, in wording that has the Prophet ﷺ put his blessed hand on the back of Sayyidna Salmān al-Fārisī, may Allah be pleased with him.

Sit with the silence. Three times the question, three times no answer — and then, instead of a name or a nation, a hand placed on one Persian man who was sitting there in the gathering. The answer to "who are the others?" was a person in the room.

Ibn Kathir says this hadith indicates that Sūrat al-Jumuʿah was revealed in Madīnah and that the Messenger's message is **universal**; and that the Prophet ﷺ explained "others among them" by mentioning Persia — which is why he ﷺ sent messages to the kings of Persia and Rome, among other kings, calling them to Allah and to follow what he was sent with. This is also why Mujāhid and several others said the phrase refers to **all non-Arabs who believe in the truth of the Prophet ﷺ**. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds a careful qualification: the narration does not specify the people of Persia — it does prove that they are included in the general sense of "others", and it speaks greatly of all non-Arabs who embrace Islam.

**Doesn't ayah 2 say he was sent to the unlettered Arabs?** Ibn Kathir addresses this head-on. Mentioning the unlettered ones specifically does not mean Muhammad ﷺ was sent only to them; the blessing to the Arabs is simply the greater one. Compare *"and verily, this is indeed a Reminder for you and your people"* (43:44) — yet the Qurʾān is surely also a reminder for those other than Arabs to take heed — and *"and warn your tribe of near kindred"* (26:214). These ayat do not negate Allah's statements: *"Say: O mankind! Verily, I am sent to you all as the Messenger of Allah"* (7:158); *"that I may therewith warn you and whomsoever it may reach"* (6:19); and, of the Qurʾān, *"but those of the groups that reject it, the Fire will be their promised meeting place"* (11:17). Ibn Kathir concludes that the Prophet ﷺ was sent to all people, mankind and jinn alike.

**A grammatical fork worth knowing.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān reports two views on what *ākharīn* is grammatically joined to, and does not force them into one:
- **View one:** it is conjoined to *ummiyyīn* — Allah has sent His Messenger ﷺ among the unlettered people *and also* among those who have not yet joined them. Sending him among the unlettered people already present is quite obvious; "sending him among those who have not yet come" needs explanation, and Bayān ul-Qurʾān explains that "sending among them" stands for "sending **for** them", because the Arabic preposition *fī* is also used in the sense of "for".
- **View two:** according to some other grammarians, *ākharīn* is conjoined to the objective pronoun *-hum* attached to the verb *yuʿallimuhum* — so the meaning is that the Prophet ﷺ teaches the unlettered people *and also* the people who have not joined them so far. Mazharī prefers this latter interpretation.

Either way, the later generations are inside the ayah, not outside it — reached by his sending, or taught by his teaching.

## Ayah 4: naming the gift

*That is the grace of Allah, which He bestows on whom He wills. And Allah is the Owner of mighty grace.* Ibn Kathir says this refers to two things: **the great prophethood that Allah granted Muhammad ﷺ**, and **the qualities that He favoured his Ummah with, by sending Muhammad ﷺ to them**.

Read against everything before it, ayah 4 leaves no ground for boasting. The Arabs did not earn a Messenger by their literacy — they had none. The later nations had not yet joined the earlier believers at all. Salmān was Persian; and even so, the Prophet ﷺ said that if faith were at the Pleiades, men from his people would attain it. Every part of it is *faḍl*: given, bestowed "on whom He wills".

## Living it

- **Join the tasbīḥ that is already underway.** Ayah 1 is in the continuous form for a reason. Stones and trees are, in their own way, declaring the purity of their Maker; the believer is the one creature invited to do it knowingly.
- **Measure yourself by the three verbs.** Recitation, purification, teaching. A relationship with the Qurʾān that has recitation but no *tazkiyah*, or knowledge but no change of character, is missing pieces that were named together among the objectives the Messenger ﷺ was sent with.
- **Take ayah 3 personally.** On what was transmitted from Ibn Zayd, Mujāhid and others, every Muslim who enters Islam until the Last Hour is one of "the others" — appended to the noble Companions, spoken of in a verse revealed before they existed. Rūḥ calls that great good news; receive it as such.
- **Drop the ranking of peoples.** The one man singled out when the Companions asked "who are they?" was not an Arab. Ibn Kathir takes the same hadith as evidence that the Messenger's message is universal, and Mujāhid and others read the ayah as covering all non-Arabs who believe in the truth of the Prophet ﷺ.

passages.title: Entrusted with the Torah but unwilling
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

Having just described the Prophet ﷺ raised up among an unlettered people with the objectives of his mission set out in the opening ayat of the surah, Allah now turns to the community that had been given a scripture long before — and had it in their hands when that same Prophet ﷺ appeared. Ayat 5–8 form one continuous argument: a parable exposing knowledge without action (ayah 5), a challenge that tests a claim (ayah 6), the silence that answers the challenge (ayah 7), and the reality nobody escapes in the end (ayah 8). The thread running through all four is the gap between what a person *claims* about his standing with Allah and what his life and his fears actually reveal.

---

## Ayah 5: the donkey and the books

**The image.** "The example of those who were entrusted with the Tawrah, but did not carry it, is as the likeness of a donkey which carries huge burdens of books." The Arabic word rendered "books" is *asfār*, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains is the plural of *sifr* — a large book, a weighty tome. So the picture is not a donkey with a light satchel; Maʿārif describes it as a donkey loaded with weighty tomes — an animal carrying enormous value on its back and receiving nothing from it.

Notice too the verb. Allah says they were *made to carry* the Tawrah (*ḥummilū*) and then *did not carry it* (*lam yaḥmilūhā*) — the same root used twice, once for the trust placed on them and once for the trust they refused. Maʿārif renders the sense as: they were ordered to bear the responsibility of *acting upon* the Torah, and did not bear it. To carry a revelation, in the Qur'anic sense, is not to transport its pages but to live under its weight.

**Why the comparison stings.** Ibn Kathir draws the point out with precision. When a donkey carries books, it cannot understand what those books contain; it is moving them by sheer strength and nothing more. That, he says, is exactly the case of those entrusted with the Tawrah: "they read its letter but did not understand its meanings nor abided by them. Rather, they even corrupted and changed the Tawrah." And then the blade turns: **they are worse than the donkey.** The donkey has no capacity to understand and is not blamed for its ignorance. They *had* minds capable of understanding — and their minds were of no benefit to them. Ibn Kathir cites the same logic from elsewhere in the Qur'an: "They are like cattle, nay even more astray; those! They are the heedless" (7:179).

**What blinded them.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supplies the historical sharpness. The Torah described the Holy Prophet ﷺ with almost the same qualities as the Qur'an describes him, which required that as soon as the Jews saw him they should have recognised him and believed in him. But, as Maʿārif puts it, "material position and possessions blinded them to the teachings of Torah." They carried the Torah around for material gain and for the status it won them among people, but did not benefit from its guidance. Despite their knowledge of the Torah they acted, in Maʿārif's phrase, as "practical ignoramus" — learned in text and illiterate in life.

**"How bad is the example of people who deny the Ayat of Allah. And Allah does not guide the people who are wrongdoers."** The ayah closes not with the parable but with a verdict, and the verdict names the cause: *ẓulm*, wrongdoing. Guidance is withheld from those who have chosen injustice — the same word that will return in ayah 7.

**This is not a parable about someone else.** The commentators themselves refuse to leave it in the past. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that commentators have stated that the example given by this verse for the Jews "applies to any religious scholar who does not act upon his knowledge," and quotes a Persian poet to drive it home:

> He is neither a scholar, nor a knowledgeable person.
> He is but an animal of four legs, carrying the load of some books.

Sit with that before moving on. A person who memorises, quotes, teaches, argues, corrects others — and does not let any of it change how he prays, earns, speaks, or treats his family — is, in the Qur'an's own image, freight, not a reader. The one protection against becoming the donkey is not knowing less; it is letting what you know cost you something.

---

## Ayat 6–7: a challenge, and the silence that answered it

**The claim being tested.** In ayah 6 the Prophet ﷺ is instructed: "Say: 'O you Jews! If you pretend that you are friends of Allah, to the exclusion of all other people, then long for death if you are truthful.'" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out what claim is in view. Despite their kufr, shirk and moral aberration they said, "We are the sons of Allah and His favourites" (5:18), and, "no one shall ever enter Paradise unless he is a Jew" (2:111). In other words, as Maʿārif puts it, they believed themselves safe and immune from the punishment of the Hereafter, and thought the blessings of Paradise were their personal property.

**Why "long for death" is the perfect test.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the reasoning with disarming simplicity. If a man genuinely believes that the blessings of the Hereafter are immeasurably better than anything in this world, and that the instant he dies he will certainly receive those numerous and eternal blessings, then wishing for death follows of necessity. He sees with his own eyes that this world is not free from miseries, sorrows and hardships, and that one has to suffer from certain diseases as long as he lives here. If death is the door out of all that and into eternal peace, a wise man would naturally wish for the door to open. So the challenge is not cruelty; it is the cleanest possible audit of a claim. Allah does not ask them to argue. He asks them to *want* what their own doctrine says is waiting for them.

Ibn Kathir gives a second, complementary reading of the challenge: 'if you claim that you are on the correct guidance and that Muhammad and his Companions are being led astray, then invoke Allah to bring death to the misguided group among the two, if you are truthful in your claim.' On this reading it is a mutual invocation — each side asks Allah to destroy whichever party is misguided, "either they or their enemies," as Ibn Kathir words it. He notes he has explained these meanings before at Surat al-Baqarah (2:94–96), where the same challenge is issued and the same refusal recorded, along with the observation that they are "the greediest of mankind for life." He also points out that the Qur'an issues parallel challenges to other groups: a similar challenge against the Christians in Sūrah Āl ʿImrān ("Come, let us call our sons and your sons… then we pray and invoke the curse of Allah upon those who lie," 3:61), and against the idolaters in Sūrah Maryam ("Say: whoever is in error, the Most Gracious will extend circumstances for him," 19:75).

**The answer arrives in ayah 7 before they can speak.** "But they will never long for it, because of what their hands have sent before them." Not *did* not — *will never*. The Qur'an closes the case in advance; Maʿārif states that, being convinced of the falsity of their position, the Jews will refuse to accept the challenge.

Ibn Kathir explains the reason given — "what their hands have sent before them" — as "the disbelief, injustice and sins that they commit." Maʿārif adds the psychological layer: they fully know that there will be nothing for them in the Hereafter but the punishment of Hell. Their claim to be Allah's children and His loved ones is absolutely false, "a claim that they themselves know is false," made for worldly and material gains. And they knew something else: that if they accepted the Prophet's ﷺ challenge and invoked death upon themselves, it would be readily accepted and they would die instantly. Maʿārif reports that a Prophetic Tradition relates from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that if any one of them at that time had wished for death, he would have died instantly (Maʿārif cites this from *Rūḥ*, without naming a ḥadīth collection).

**A striking narration.** Ibn Kathir records here that Imam Ahmad transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that Abu Jahl said, "If I see Muhammad praying at the Kaʿbah, I will step on his neck." When the Prophet ﷺ heard of this he said: "Had he done so, the angels would have snatched him away in public. Had the Jews wished for death, they would all have perished and saw their seats in Hellfire. Had those accepted for invoking the curse of Allah with Allah's Messenger, they would not have found families or property when they returned home." Ibn Kathir notes that al-Bukhari, at-Tirmidhi and an-Nasa'i recorded it. Three conditionals sit in one sentence, and each of them describes something that never happened: Abu Jahl never took the step, the Jews never wished for death, and those invited to invoke the curse of Allah alongside the Messenger of Allah ﷺ never accepted. One pattern runs through all three — the loudest claims retreat the moment they are asked to stand behind an outcome.

**"And Allah knows well the wrongdoers."** The ayah ends by returning to Allah's knowledge. He is not persuaded by claims; He knows what the hands sent ahead. This is a comfort as much as a warning: reputation is not the standard, and no one is graded on his self-description.

---

## Is it permissible to long for death?

The passage seems to command longing for death — so does that make it praiseworthy? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses this directly and answers no. This subject, it says, "has been fully discussed in Surah Al-Baqarah," and "Traditions forbid anyone to wish for death." The most important reason it gives is precisely the disease this passage is exposing: **no one has the right to believe that as soon as he dies he will certainly enter Paradise and will have no fear of any punishment.** Wishing for death in such a state of mind, Maʿārif says, "is tantamount to show bravery before Allah" — a kind of swagger in front of one's Lord.

So the challenge in ayah 6 is not a recommendation being extended to believers. It is a test aimed at a specific claim of guaranteed salvation. A believer who does not make that claim has no business longing for death; his posture is hope mixed with fear, not certainty of acquittal.

---

## Ayah 8: the appointment nobody misses

"Say: 'Verily, the death from which you flee will surely meet you, then you will be sent back to the Knower of the unseen and the seen, and He will inform you about what you used to do.'"

**The logic of the closing.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān connects it back tightly: their running away from longing for death, in spite of their claim, is tantamount to running away from death itself. So the Prophet ﷺ is instructed to tell them that the death they are fleeing would inevitably catch up with them. If not instantly, then certainly sometime later — it is impossible for anyone to avoid or avert death in any way. Ibn Kathir places alongside it the ayah of Sūrat an-Nisāʾ: "Wheresoever you may be, death will overtake you even if you are in fortresses built up strong and high" (4:78).

Feel the verb: death *meets* you (*mulāqīkum*). It is not depicted as a pit you might stumble into but as someone coming toward you, keeping an appointment. Running is simply movement toward the meeting point.

**And then the meeting after the meeting.** Death is not the end of the sentence in ayah 8; it is the middle. "Then you will be sent back to the Knower of the unseen and the seen, and He will inform you about what you used to do." Of all the names Allah could have used here, He chooses *ʿĀlim al-ghayb wa'sh-shahāda* — the One who knows the unseen and the seen. That name is the exact answer to this passage. These were people whose scripture was on display and whose lives ignored it; who made claims about their standing with Allah that, as Maʿārif says, they themselves knew to be false. The One they return to knows both halves. Nothing curated survives the journey, and He Himself will be the one to inform them about what they used to do.

---

## Fleeing danger is not fleeing death

A practical question follows naturally, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises it: if the ayah condemns fleeing from death, is it wrong to avoid danger?

No. There are many normal causes of death which both reason and the Sharīʿah require a person to avoid. Maʿārif mentions that the Holy Prophet ﷺ once passed under a bent wall — as if it were about to fall down or collapse — and passed it quickly, lest it collapse on him. Likewise if fire breaks out at some place, both reason and the Sharīʿah dictate that one should run away from there.

Such fleeing does not fall under the fleeing denounced in the ayah, **provided our faith is sound**: that when the predetermined time of our death approaches, we will not be able to escape. Maʿārif's reasoning is elegant — since we do not know for sure whether fire, or poison, or some other obnoxious thing will be the destined cause of our death in a particular situation, running away from it does not amount to fleeing the death the verse denounces. It is ordinary prudence within a decree we do not know.

Maʿārif notes that bubonic plague or epidemic is a separate issue, with details in the books of jurisprudence and ḥadīth, an exhaustive discussion by the author of *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī* at this point, and some details already given in Maʿārif itself under 2:243–244.

---

## What to carry away

Ayat 5–8 hand a believer three things to check in himself, all of them borrowed from a rebuke aimed at someone else:

1. **Am I carrying my Book, or transporting it?** The measure is not how much is on your back but how much has entered your life. Maʿārif applies this to every religious scholar who does not act upon his knowledge — and by extension to every one of us who knows more than we practise.
2. **Would my claim survive a test?** These people were undone not by an argument but by being asked to want what they said they believed. Our claims about trusting Allah, loving the Hereafter, or fearing Him are tested the same way, by what we actually reach for.
3. **Am I living toward the meeting?** Death is coming to meet me, and beyond it stands the One who knows the unseen and the seen and will inform me about what I used to do. That is not a reason to long for death — the sources explicitly warn against that — but it is every reason to make the hidden half of my life worth being told about.

passages.title: The Friday call, trade, and the caravan
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat legislate the Friday congregation and then correct the community's first failure to honour it. Ayah 9 calls the believers away from the marketplace to the mosque; ayah 10 sends them back out into the marketplace once the prayer is done; ayah 11 recalls the Friday a caravan pulled most of the congregation out of the mosque while the Prophet ﷺ was still on his feet. The thread running through all three is a single question: **when the call of Allah and the call of trade sound at the same moment, which one moves you?**

## Ayah 9: "When the call is proclaimed"

**Why the day is called Jumuʿah.** Ibn Kathir explains that *al-Jumuʿah* comes from *al-jamʿ*, literally *gathering* — because the people of Islam gather every week, on this day, in the major places of worship. He collects what the authentic collections report about the day: on a Friday Allah completed the creation, the sixth day; on a Friday Adam was created and placed in Paradise, and on a Friday he was taken out of it; on a Friday the Last Hour will begin; and there is an hour within Friday in which no believing servant asks Allah for something good except that Allah gives it to him.

Ibn Kathir adds a striking observation: earlier nations *were* informed about Friday, but were led astray from it. The Jews chose Saturday, though Adam was not created then; the Christians chose Sunday, the day creation began. Allah chose Friday for this Ummah — the day creation was finished. Al-Bukhari and Muslim record from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "We are the last (to come) but the first on the Day of Resurrection, though the former nations were given the Scriptures before us. And this was their day, the celebration of which was made compulsory for them, but they differed about it. So Allah gave us guidance to it, and all other people are coming after us: the Jews tomorrow and the Christians the day after tomorrow."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the pre-Islamic background. In the Days of Ignorance the day was called *Yawm al-ʿArūbah*. The first Arab to rename it *Yawm al-Jumuʿah* was Kaʿb ibn Luʼayy, one of the Prophet's ﷺ forefathers, who gathered the Quraysh on this day and addressed them some 560 years before the Prophet ﷺ came; Maʿārif notes from Mazhari that Allah kept him from idol worship and that he gave people glad tidings of the Prophet's ﷺ advent. And on the authority of Muhammad ibn Sirin, Maʿārif reports that the Ansar of Madinah had been gathering to pray on Fridays before the Hijrah — on the basis of their own *ijtihād*, which Maʿārif itself glosses simply as *their own assessment* — before Jumuʿah was made obligatory. So this ayah was not inventing a day out of nothing — it was giving divine command to a day already heavy with meaning.

## "Hasten" — a word that does not mean rushing

The command is **fas-ʿaw**, usually translated "hasten." Ibn Kathir is explicit: the *saʿy* here "does not refer to walking quickly. It only refers to the importance of it" — that is, *go to it, head for it*, treat it as urgent business. He notes that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn Masʿud (may Allah be pleased with them) recited it as *fa-mdū ilā dhikri-llāh* — "then **proceed** to the remembrance of Allah" — a reading that removes any suggestion of running.

And running is in fact forbidden. The Two Sahihs record from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said, "When you hear the Iqamah, proceed to offer the prayer with calmness and solemnity and do not rush. And pray whatever you catch, and complete whatever you have missed." (This is Al-Bukhari's wording.) The Two Sahihs also record Abu Qatadah's account: they were praying behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he heard a commotion. Afterwards he asked, "What is the matter with you?" They said, "We hastened to the prayer." He ﷺ said, "Don't do that. When you come for prayer, there should be tranquility upon you."

Al-Hasan draws the lesson out: "By Allah! Hastening to the prayer is not accomplished by the feet… Rather it is about the hearts, the intention, and the submission." Qatadah says the ayah means "you have to hasten to the prayer with your heart and actions, and walk to it."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same two senses of *saʿy* — to run, and to attend to a task consciously — and settles on the second, with a memorable image: **just as a person running towards something pays no heed to anything else, a Muslim after the call should pay attention to nothing besides the adhan and the khutbah** (the *khutbah* being the Friday sermon). The urgency is real; it simply lives in the chest and the schedule, not in the feet.

## "The remembrance of Allah" — the khutbah as well as the prayer

*Dhikr Allah* here could mean the Jumuʿah prayer, or the sermon. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Mazhari and others) judges it most appropriate to read it as the whole package — prayer *and* sermon together — noting that the sermon is one of the conditions for the validity of the Jumuʿah prayer. That matters directly for ayah 11: leaving during the khutbah is leaving the very thing you were summoned to.

## "And leave off business"

Maʿārif observes a fine point of wording: the literal sense of *bayʿ* is **selling**, not buying — yet the intent is to stop all trade. Why name only one side? Because trade is bilateral: if no one sells, no one can buy. And practically, buyers are beyond counting and cannot all be policed, whereas sellers and shopkeepers are limited — shut the shops at that hour and the market stops of itself.

Maʿārif then widens the ruling in a "Special Note": the jurists of the Ummah agree unanimously that *bayʿ* here stands for **anything that hinders preparing for and proceeding to the Jumuʿah prayer** — trading, labour, farming, and beyond that even eating, drinking, sleeping, chatting, and studying once the adhan has gone. Only what relates to Jumuʿah may be carried on.

Ibn Kathir's summary of *dhālikum khayrun lakum* ("that is better for you") is worth holding onto: your abandoning buying and selling, and concentrating instead on Allah's remembrance and the prayer, is better for you **in this life and in the Hereafter** — if only you knew. The ayah does not deny that closing the shop costs something. It says the accounting is wrong.

## Which call is meant?

Ibn Kathir: the call in the ayah is the adhan that immediately precedes the khutbah — in the Prophet's ﷺ time it was called near the door of the mosque, before him, once he had come out and sat on the *minbar*, the raised pulpit from which the sermon is given. Al-Bukhari records from as-Saʼib ibn Yazid that in the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Bakr and ʿUmar, the Friday adhan was pronounced while the Imam sat on the pulpit; but in ʿUthman's later time, when the Muslims increased in number, an additional call was pronounced upon az-Zawraʼ — the tallest house in Madinah, near the mosque.

Maʿārif explains the reasoning: Madinah's Muslim population had grown and spread to the outskirts, and the adhan given before the Imam could no longer be heard at a distance, so ʿUthman (may Allah be pleased with him) instituted an earlier call from the trading area further from the mosque, at his house at az-Zawraʼ, audible across the city. **No Companion objected**, and so it became established by their consensus — and with it, Maʿārif says, the prohibitions of this ayah now attach from that first adhan. Ibn Kathir states that the scholars of Islam agree it is forbidden to trade after the second adhan.

**A note on scope.** Maʿārif is careful that this obligation is not universal in the way the five daily prayers are. Jumuʿah replaces Zuhr by consensus of the Ummah, but unlike the daily prayers it is not valid without a congregation, and the jurists differ on how many people that requires. It is not obligatory on women, the sick, or travellers, who pray Zuhr instead, and by no jurist's view is it valid in desert or wilderness. Imam ash-Shafiʿi requires forty free, sane, adult men resident in the locality; Imam Malik requires adjoining houses and a market; Imam Abu Hanifah requires a town, city, or very large village with streets, markets, a Muslim ruler and a judge able to settle disputes. Maʿārif's conclusion is pastoral: the disagreement is only over identifying the prerequisites — wherever they apply, neglecting Jumuʿah without a valid reason in terms of the Sharīʿah carries grave warning, and fulfilling it carries the promise of great reward.

## From the Sunnah: how to come

Ibn Kathir gathers the etiquette of the day around this ayah. Ghusl — the full washing of the body — before coming is emphasised: the Two Sahihs record from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "When one of you comes to the Friday prayer, then let him perform bath"; and from Abu Saʿid, "Ghusl on the day of Jumuʿah is *wajib* (required) from every *muhtalim*." Muslim records from Abu Hurayrah that it is Allah's right on every Muslim to bathe every seven days, washing head and body; Ahmad, an-Nasaʼi and Ibn Hibban record the like from Jabir, naming that day as Friday.

Ibn Kathir then lists what is recommended: cleaning the body, ghusl, one's best clothes, perfume, and the siwak (tooth-stick) — Abu Saʿid's narration itself mentions the siwak and one's household's perfume. Imam Ahmad records from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari that whoever performs ghusl on Friday, applies perfume if he has any, wears his best clothes, goes to the mosque, prays voluntarily if he wishes, **does not bother anyone**, and listens silently once the Imam appears until he prays — all of this is an expiation for what falls between that Friday and the next. Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah record from ʿAbdullah ibn Salam that the Prophet ﷺ said from the minbar: what harm would it do for one of you to buy two garments for Friday, besides his daily working clothes?

On coming early, Imam Ahmad records from Aws ibn Aws ath-Thaqafi that whoever performs ghusl well on Friday, sets out early, walks rather than rides, sits close to the Imam and listens without idle talk, earns for every step the reward of a year's fasting and night prayer; Ibn Kathir notes the compilers of the Four Sunan collected it and at-Tirmidhi graded it *hasan* (a recognised grade of soundness). And the Two Sahihs record from Abu Hurayrah the image of the hours: whoever comes in the first hour is as one who offered a camel, the second a cow, the third a horned ram, the fourth a hen, the fifth an egg — "and when the Imam appears, the angels present themselves to listen to Allah's remembrance." The one who left with the caravan in ayah 11 walked out on that gathering.

## Ayah 10: dispersal is not a retreat

Ibn Kathir: having forbidden work after the adhan and commanded the gathering, Allah then permits them to spread through the earth and seek His bounty once the prayer is finished — a section Maʿārif titles "Blessings in Business after Jumuʿah". The marketplace is not the enemy of the mosque; it is ordered after it.

Both commentaries preserve an illustration recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim: when the Friday prayer ended, ʿIrak ibn Malik would stand at the gate of the mosque and pray, "O Allah! I have accepted and complied with Your Call, performed the prayer You ordered and dispersed as You ordered me. Therefore, grant me of Your favor, and You are the best of those who grant provisions." He turned his walk to work into obedience — the *dispersing* itself done "as You ordered me". Maʿārif adds, from the righteous elders as cited by Ibn Kathir, that whoever conducts his trade after the Jumuʿah prayer is favoured by Allah with seventy blessings.

Then comes the safeguard: **"and remember Allah much, that you may be successful."** Ibn Kathir reads it precisely — while you are buying and selling, giving and taking, remember Allah much, and do not let this life busy you from what benefits you in the Hereafter. Maʿārif puts it as not neglecting Allah's remembrance during commerce "as the infidels do". Ibn Kathir cites a hadith — without naming its collection — that whoever enters a marketplace and says, "*Lā ilāha illa-llāh, alone without partners; His is the sovereignty and His is the praise, and He is able to do all things*," Allah records for him a thousand thousand good deeds and erases a thousand thousand evil deeds. Mujahid sets the bar for "much": a servant is not among those who remember Allah often until he does so standing, sitting, and lying down.

## Ayah 11: the caravan, and the twelve who stayed

Ibn Kathir: Allah is criticising what happened on one Friday, when a caravan arrived at Madinah and the people rushed out to the merchandise, leaving the Messenger of Allah ﷺ standing. Several of the Tabiʿin — the generation that came after the Companions — said "standing" means on the minbar, delivering the khutbah; among them Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Hasan, Zayd ibn Aslam and Qatadah. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said the caravan belonged to Dihyah ibn Khalifah before he became a Muslim, and drums came with it.

Imam Ahmad records from Jabir: "Once, a caravan arrived at Al-Madinah while Allah's Messenger ﷺ was giving a Khutbah. So the people left, and only twelve men remained." Then this ayah came down. Ibn Kathir notes the Two Sahihs also recorded it; Maʿārif cites the figure of twelve from a narration in the *Marāsīl* of Abu Dawud.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds detail and, importantly, **excuses that are not excuses**. Muqatil (whom Maʿārif calls the leading scholar of Qurʼanic commentary) says this was Dihyah ibn Khalaf al-Kalbi's trading caravan from Syria; it normally brought essentials, above all foodstuffs, and drums were beaten to announce it, so men and women alike would rush to it. Dihyah was not yet a Muslim; he accepted Islam later. Al-Hasan al-Basri and Abu Malik said this was a time of scarcity and dearth. Maʿārif lists the factors: the *fard* (obligatory) prayer had already finished; the Companions did not yet know whether the sermon was part of the obligation; goods were genuinely scarce; and they feared that if they were late, the essentials would be gone. Humanly understandable — and still, Maʿārif says plainly, the Companions committed a mistake, and this ayah was revealed to admonish them and put them to shame. According to some narratives, transmitted by Abu Yaʿla and quoted by Ibn Kathir, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"If all had gone, the entire valley of Madinah would have been filled with the fire of punishment."** Notice the grammar of that warning: it is a conditional, not a report of what occurred. What we are told is that some stayed.

**A change in practice.** Maʿārif reports Ibn Kathir's position that at that time the Prophet ﷺ delivered the Friday sermon *after* the prayer — as is still done on the two ʿIds — and that from that day he ﷺ changed the order, delivering the sermon first; this is the approved Sunnah. Ibn Kathir also draws a ruling from the words *tarakūka qāʼiman* ("they left you **standing**"): it proves the Imam should deliver the Friday sermon standing. Muslim records in his *Sahih* from Jabir ibn Samurah that the Prophet ﷺ gave two sermons and sat between them, reciting the Qurʼan and reminding the people.

**The answer given.** Allah does not argue with them about the price of grain. He tells His Prophet ﷺ to say: *what is with Allah is better than the amusement and the merchandise, and Allah is the best of providers.* Ibn Kathir: "what Allah has" means the reward with Him in the Hereafter, and He is the best of providers **for those who trust in Him and seek His provision when they are permitted to do so** — which is precisely the permission ayah 10 had just granted. The rebuke is not against seeking sustenance. It is against seeking it out of turn, from a source you imagined was more reliable than the One who sends the caravans.

Maʿārif closes on the same note of trust: it is not far-fetched that those who leave off business for the prayer and sermon will draw ample blessing into their provision even in this world.

## Living it

- **When the call goes, the shop closes.** Not a jog to the mosque — a life arranged so the hour is already free. Al-Hasan: the hastening is of the heart, the intention, the submission.
- **Come as a guest of the day.** Ghusl, siwak, clean clothes, perfume if you have it, early, walking, close to the Imam, harming no one, silent once he stands — the angels are listening with you.
- **Go back out afterwards as an act of worship.** Take ʿIrak ibn Malik's prayer at the door with you: *I answered Your call, I prayed, I am dispersing as You commanded — now provide for me from Your bounty.* And keep Allah on your tongue in the market itself, where this passage began and where it deliberately ends.
